questions.q: In a multi-tenant Task API, what is a tenant?
questions.explain: Acme and Globex are tenants. Each has its own users and tasks, but they all use one copy of the application and, with shared tables, one database.
options: One user account
One customer, such as a company, that shares the same application with other customers
One server that runs a copy of the app
One database table

questions.q: What is the most important rule of multi-tenancy?
questions.explain: This is tenant isolation. A bug here is not small: it shows one company's data to another company, possibly a competitor.
options: Every tenant must have its own server
A request from one tenant must never read or change another tenant's data
Tenant names must be secret
Each tenant must use a different programming language

questions.q: The Task API uses shared tables: every row has a tenant_id column. What is the main risk of this strategy?
questions.explain: Shared tables are the cheapest and simplest to run, but every query must filter on tenant_id. That is why the repository adds the filter itself instead of trusting each caller.
options: It is the most expensive strategy
Migrations must run once per tenant
One forgotten tenant_id filter in a query leaks data
It cannot store more than one tenant

questions.q: Which strategy gives the strongest isolation, and is usually kept for large customers because it costs the most?
questions.explain: A whole database per tenant has the strongest walls but the highest cost. Schema per tenant sits in between. Shared tables are the usual starting point.
options: Shared tables with a tenant_id column
Schema per tenant
Database per tenant
One table per user

questions.q: Initech did not pay, and its tenant status is suspended. What should happen when an Initech user sends a request?
questions.explain: manager.requireActive(id) loads the tenant and throws TenantUnavailableError when it is not active. The user logged in before the suspension, but that does not matter.
options: It works, because the user is logged in
It is refused: only active tenants may use the app
It works in read-only mode automatically
The user is moved to another tenant

questions.q: Why must a tenant id like acme:admin be refused?
questions.explain: Characters like :, / and .. have a meaning inside keys and paths. A strict pattern keeps every tenant id a plain, safe name.
options: Colons make the id too long
Tenant ids end up in cache keys, file paths and log lines; such an id could forge a key that belongs to someone else
JavaScript strings cannot contain colons
The database cannot store it

questions.q: What is tenant resolution?
questions.explain: Every request must be tied to one tenant. Resolvers do this, each looking at a different part of the request: the session, the host name, a header or the path.
options: Deleting tenants that no longer pay
Finding out which tenant a request belongs to
Choosing the database strategy
Merging two tenants into one

questions.q: Which list gives the lesson's trust levels correctly?
questions.explain: Your server created the session when the user logged in, so its tenant is trusted. A header or path is written by the client, so it is untrusted.
options: Header: trusted. Subdomain: verified. Session: untrusted.
Session or token claim: trusted. Subdomain or domain: verified. Header or path: untrusted.
All resolvers are trusted once the user is logged in.
Session: verified. Header: trusted. Path: verified.

questions.q: Why is an x-tenant-id header sent by the client untrusted?
questions.explain: If your app believed the header, every Acme user could read Globex's tasks by adding one line to their request. The tenant must come from something your server created, like the session.
options: Headers are often lost by proxies
Headers cannot contain lower-case letters
The client writes it: anybody can send x-tenant-id: globex with curl
Headers are encrypted, so the server cannot read them

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The session claim is trusted. The header-only request still finds globex, but marks it untrusted, so the next check can refuse it.
options:
acme jwt trusted
globex header untrusted

acme jwt trusted
globex header trusted

acme jwt verified
globex header verified

acme jwt trusted
globex jwt trusted

questions.q: ada from Acme is logged in and also sends x-tenant-id: globex. What does this print?
questions.explain: The chain asks by priority, and the JWT resolver has the highest. It answers first, so the header is never even read. The trusted session wins.
options: acme trusted
globex untrusted
globex trusted
acme untrusted

questions.q: This chain lists the header resolver first. What does this print?
questions.explain: A resolver chain asks its resolvers in order of priority, not in the order of the array. The JWT resolver has the highest priority, so the trusted session still wins.
options: acme jwt
globex header
acme header
globex jwt

questions.q: In a resolver chain, the JWT resolver throws because the token is invalid. What happens?
questions.explain: If a broken token fell through to the next resolver, an attacker could send a bad token plus an x-tenant-id header. Stopping the chain closes that door.
options: The chain skips it and asks the header resolver
The whole chain stops with the error; a failed login can never fall through to the header
The chain returns the default tenant
The chain retries the JWT resolver

questions.q: A tenant check fails. What should the client receive?
questions.explain: An attacker probing tenant names should not learn which ones exist or are suspended. Log the reason on the server; send the client only "Forbidden".
options: The exact reason, like "tenant initech is suspended"
A list of valid tenant names
A plain 403 without the reason
A 200 with an empty list

questions.explain: Every tenancy error extends TenantError, which is an AuthorizationError from @zudojs/errors, so it already carries status 403.
options: true 403
false 403

questions.q: When is it acceptable to resolve the tenant from an x-tenant-id header?
questions.explain: Then the header was written by your proxy, not by the client, and you create the resolver with createHeaderResolver({ trust: "verified" }). The app must never be reachable without that proxy.
options: When the value passes tryCreateTenantId
When the request uses HTTPS
Only when a proxy you control removes the client's header and sets its own, for example after checking an API key
When the tenant is active

questions.q: A developer suggests choosing the tenant with ?tenant=acme. Is that safe on its own?
questions.explain: Validating the id only checks its format, not who may use it. Anything the client writes is untrusted; the tenant must come from the verified session or a key your server issued.
options: Yes, because query parameters are part of the URL
Yes, if the tenant id is validated
No: the client writes it, like a header, so it is untrusted
Yes, for GET requests

questions.q: A partner system calls your API with an API key. How should you find its tenant?
questions.explain: The key was created by your server and stored with its tenant. Looking up the tenant from the key is like reading it from a session.
options: Ask the partner to send x-tenant-id with each call
Look the tenant up from the API key on the server: trusted, because your server issued the key
Read it from the partner's IP address
Use the first tenant in the database

questions.q: A user logged in to Acme opens globex.tasks.test. What does this print?
questions.explain: With detectConflicts: true, the chain asks all resolvers and throws when they disagree. The session says Acme, the subdomain says Globex: that is refused.
options: TenantResolutionConflictError 403
tenant: acme
tenant: globex
TenantTrustLevelError 403

questions.q: Why does the tenancy package keep the current tenant in an AsyncLocalStorage instead of passing it as a parameter?
questions.explain: Services, repositories, cache keys and log lines all need the tenant. AsyncLocalStorage gives each request's async chain its own value, so code reads it without a parameter to forget.
options: Parameters are slower
Passing it through every function is tedious, and one forgotten parameter is a leak
So the client can change it
So every request shares the same tenant

listing tasks of Globex
listing tasks of Acme

listing tasks of Acme
listing tasks of Globex

listing tasks of Globex
listing tasks of Globex

listing tasks of Acme

questions.q: Which repository method is written the safe way?
questions.explain: The repository reads the tenant from the context itself, so callers cannot pass a wrong one, and the id goes in as a parameter, never glued into the SQL text. Filtering later is one forgotten line away from a leak.
options: db.query(`select * from tasks where tenant_id = '${tenantId}'`)
list(tenantId) { return db.query("select * from tasks where tenant_id = $1", [tenantId]) }, called with a tenant from the request body
db.query("select id, title from tasks where tenant_id = $1", [tenantContext.requireCurrentTenant().id])
db.query("select id, title from tasks"), then filter in the handler

questions.q: Why does get(id) use where id = $1 and tenant_id = $2 and not only where id = $1?
questions.explain: The id alone identifies a row in the whole table, across all tenants. Adding tenant_id to the lookup means another tenant's row is simply not found.
options: It makes the query faster
Ids count up and are easy to guess; without the tenant filter, Acme could read Globex's task 2
Postgres requires two conditions
So the query returns two rows

questions.q: Acme asks for GET /tasks/2, and task 2 belongs to Globex. Which status should the API answer?
questions.explain: For the client, "belongs to someone else" and "does not exist" must look the same. A 403 would tell an attacker that the id exists.
options: 403, because Acme may not see it
404, exactly like an id that does not exist
200 with Globex's task, because the id is valid
500, because something is wrong

questions.q: You add rename(id, title) to the repository. What must its update query contain?
questions.explain: Writes need the tenant filter just as much as reads. Without it, Acme could rename or delete Globex's task by guessing its id.
options: Only where id = $2, because the reads already check the tenant
where id = $2 and tenant_id = $3, with the tenant from the context
The tenant name in the new title
Nothing special: updates cannot leak data

questions.q: In the final Task API, a request has x-tenant-id: globex but no session. What happens?
questions.explain: The handler finds the session first. No session means 401 before tenant resolution runs.
options: It lists Globex's tasks, because the header names a tenant
401: the request is not logged in, so the header is not even looked at
403: the header is untrusted

questions.explain: manager.requireActive throws a TenantError, and the server turns every TenantError into a plain 403 without details.
options: 200: the session is still valid
401: the user must log in again
A plain 403 {"error":"Forbidden"} without the reason
404 with the message "tenant suspended"

questions.q: Finish cleanTenantId(raw): trim and lower-case the text, then return it only if it matches ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*$; otherwise return undefined. The program should print acme undefined undefined acme-eu.
questions.explain: Normalize first, then validate against a strict pattern anchored with ^ and $. Ids with :, . or / could forge cache keys or paths.

questions.q: Finish meetsTrust(actual, required): the levels from low to high are untrusted, verified, trusted. Return true when actual is at least required. The program should print true true false false.
questions.explain: A higher level also satisfies a lower requirement. An untrusted answer, like a client header, never reaches verified.

questions.q: Finish tenantFor(request): use request.session.tenantId when there is a session. Never use request.headers["x-tenant-id"]. Without a session, return "DENY". The program should print acme acme DENY.
questions.explain: The session was created by your server at login, so its tenant is trusted. The header is written by the client: ada's x-tenant-id: globex changes nothing, and a header without a session gets nothing.

questions.q:
Finish listTasks(tenantId) and getTask(tenantId, id) so they only ever return rows of that tenant. The program should print:

[ { id: 1, title: 'Acme: ship order 1001' } ]
undefined
questions.explain: Both lookups must check the tenant, just like where id = $1 and tenant_id = $2. Acme guessing Globex's id 2 finds nothing.

questions.q: Finish statusFor(tenantId, id): return 200 when the task exists and belongs to the tenant; otherwise return 404, whether the task is missing or belongs to someone else. The program should print 200 404 404.
questions.explain: Another tenant's task and a missing task give the same 404. A 403 for task 2 would tell an attacker that id 2 exists.

questions.q:

true false
[ 'Acme task, renamed', 'Globex task' ]
questions.explain: Writes need the tenant check as much as reads. Acme's attempt on Globex's task changes nothing and reports false.
